deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three separate pieces.

(A) Joule heat, at the top. W J^2 is the heat developed by a current J in a conductor of resistance W. The volume form is ∭ w c^2 dS = ∫ i Π cos(ζ,Π) dS, where w is the specific resistance and c the current density. Riemann glosses it as 'the work done in the time element dt, i.e. the living force lost'. The right-hand side reads as a surface integral of a potential-type quantity times the normal component of the current. This is the energy balance of a stationary current: Joule dissipation equals the work done by the driving forces, written as a boundary integral. The next page continues it: ∭ w ε^2 dS = W J^2, and ½Σ ε m v^2 − P − ∫(X dx+Y dy+Z dz) = const.

(B) Two circles as Apollonian circles of one pair of points (middle of the page). Let z' be the conjugate of z. The equation (z−μ)/(z−λ) · (z'−μ)/(z'−λ) = p is the circle |z−μ|^2 = p|z−λ|^2.
1. Expanding gives (1−p) z z' − (μ−λp)(z+z') + (μ^2−λ^2 p) = 0.
2. The value p = μ/λ gives (1−μ/λ) z z' + μ(μ−λ) = 0, i.e. z z' = λμ. So the circle |z| = a has λ, μ as inverse points exactly when λμ = a^2.
3. Put q = 1−p and divide by q. Compare with the general circle z z' − c(z+z') + cc − bb = 0 (centre c, radius b). This gives:
   - (μ−λ)/q + λ = c,
   - (μ^2−λ^2)/q + λ^2 = cc − bb.
4. Eliminating q: (μ+λ)(c−λ) + λ^2 = cc − bb.
5. With μ = aa/λ: aa(c/λ − 1) + λc = cc − bb, hence a/λ + λ/a = (cc − bb + aa)/(ca).
This fixes the common pair of inverse points (the limiting points of the coaxal family) of the circles |z| = a and |z−c| = b.

Special case of equal radii, b = a = r = 1 (normalised): λ + 1/λ = c. Then v = log((z−λ)/(z−1/λ)) is a complex potential whose real part is constant on both circles.
- On z = e^{iφ} the modulus of the quotient is λ, so Re v = log λ.
- On z = c − e^{iφ}, using c − λ = 1/λ and c − 1/λ = λ, v = log((1/λ − e^{iφ})/(λ − e^{iφ})) (Riemann writes the denominator as re^{φi} − λ, which only adds iπ). So Re v = −log λ.
- Restoring r: λ + 1/λ = c/r. Setting 2r/c = sin ψ gives λ = tan(ψ/2), since tan(ψ/2) + cot(ψ/2) = 2/sin ψ.
- The two equipotential values are ± log tan(ψ/2). The marks 1/2 and −1/2 presumably normalise the potential to ±1/2 on the two electrodes.
- Equivalently log(1/λ) = arccosh(c/2r). This gives the resistance between two equal circular electrodes in an infinite plate (or the capacity of two parallel cylinders).

(C) Potential of a closed current: a double layer (lower part).
1. Conditions: div(X,Y,Z) = 0 and ∂X/∂y − ∂Y/∂x = 0 (etc.), so ∫X dx + Y dy + Z dz = 0 around closed curves where the field is irrotational.
2. Potential sought: harmonic (ΔV = 0), with a constant jump V_{+0} − V_{−0} = A across a surface spanning the circuit, and continuous normal derivative.
3. Realisation as a double layer: densities ∓A/(4πε) dS on two sheets a distance ε apart. This gives V' = (1/4π) ∫ A ∂(1/r)/∂n dS, i.e. A/(4π) times the solid angle subtended (marked 'dω').
4. Physical statement, in German on the page: ∫(X dx + Y dy + Z dz) taken right-to-left around the surface equals the quantity of electricity flowing upward through the surface (per unit time) times a constant. This is the circuital law, with the circulation equal to the jump A.
5. Proof of the infinitesimal circulation theorem on a rectangle dx dy (my reconstruction of the terms): X dx + Y_{x+dx} dy − X_{y+dy} dx − Y dy = (∂Y/∂x − ∂X/∂y) dx dy. Riemann omits dx dy.
The next page extends this to a general surface z = z(x,y), i.e. Stokes' theorem, and proves the double-layer representation via Green's formula.
errors: The normalisation λ + 1/λ = c/a (later c/r) holds only for equal radii b = a; Riemann silently specialises from the general a/λ + λ/a = (cc−bb+aa)/(ca).
On the second circle Riemann writes the denominator as (re^{φi} − λ) instead of (λ − re^{φi}). This is a sign, i.e. an additive iπ in v, and does not affect Re v.

In the expansion on |z| = 1 the logarithmic term should be log((1−λe^{−iφ})/(1−λe^{iφ})) + iφ (+ iπ). The transcribed form appears inverted or garbled. Since that factor has modulus 1, the conclusion Re v = log λ is unaffected.
The rectangle computation drops the factor dx dy on the right-hand side, which is harmless.

results.what: Joule heat ∭ w c^2 dS = W J^2 equated to the work of the driving forces (energy balance of stationary currents)
results.modern_name: Joule's law / energy theorem for steady currents

results.what: Determination of the common inverse (limiting) points λ, μ of two circles via λμ = a^2 and a/λ + λ/a = (c^2 − b^2 + a^2)/(ca)
results.modern_name: Limiting points of a coaxal (Apollonian) pencil of circles

results.what: Complex potential log((z−λ)/(z−1/λ)) with Re v = ± log tan(ψ/2) on two equal circles, sin ψ = 2r/c
results.modern_name: Bipolar coordinates; resistance between two circular electrodes in a plate / capacitance of two parallel cylinders (arccosh(c/2r))
results.usually_credited_to: Kirchhoff (1845–46, current in plates); Thomson (images of cylinders)

results.what: Potential of a closed current as a double layer: jump A across a spanning surface, V' = (A/4π) × solid angle
results.modern_name: Ampère's equivalence of current loop and magnetic shell; double-layer potential

results.what: Circulation of the force around a closed curve equals a constant times the current through any spanning surface, proved infinitesimally on a rectangle
results.modern_name: Ampère's circuital law; Stokes' theorem (infinitesimal form)

deep.surprise_reason: Standard lecture-level material: coaxal circles, a 2D potential between two cylinders, the double layer for a current loop, and the infinitesimal Stokes argument. The double-layer and circulation treatment appears in Riemann's published lectures (Hattendorff, 'Schwere, Elektricität und Magnetismus'). Plate-current problems were contemporary work of Kirchhoff and others.

checkable.asserts: p = μ/λ gives the circle z z' = λμ
Coefficient identities after dividing by q = 1 − p
Final relation a/λ + λ/a = (cc − bb + aa)/(ca)
λ = tan(ψ/2) solves λ + 1/λ = c/r when sin ψ = 2r/c
On |z| = 1, |(z−λ)/(z−1/λ)| = λ, so Re v = log λ (numerical check, λ = 0.3)
On |z − c| = 1 with c = λ + 1/λ, the modulus is 1/λ, so Re v = −log λ

transcription_corrections: '(1−μ/λ)zz' + μ(c−λ)' should read '(1−μ/λ)zz' + μ(μ−λ)', which is what p = μ/λ gives.

'V_{+0} − V_{−0} = π' and '∫X dx + Y dy + Z dz = π': the constant is almost certainly a letter A (Fraktur 𝔄), matching 'U_{+0} − U_{−0} = A' on the next page. Likewise 'dμ = ∓π/(4πε) dS' should be ∓A/(4πε) dS, and 'π/4π ∫…' should be A/4π ∫….
'V' = … = π/2' is doubtful; the context (marked dω) indicates the result is (A/4π) × solid angle.
The rectangle line should read 'X dx + Y_{x+dx} dy − X_{y+dy} dx − Y dy = (∂Y/∂x − ∂X/∂y)(dx dy)'; the leading 'Y_x dy − X dx' is a misreading.
'λ + 1/λ = c/a[?]' is a plausible reading but valid only for b = a; later it is used as c/r.
In the |z| = 1 expansion the fraction is likely (1−λe^{−φi})/(1−λe^{φi}) (or written inversely with a sign); uncertain.
Top line: 'W 𝔍^2' (J = current intensity); 'c^2' in ∭ w c^2 dS may be ε^2 (the current density, as on the next page).
